captions.text: A grid is made from lines, spaces between the lines,
and points where the lines meet.
These are three different things to count.
For a rectangle on a grid, choose the two lines that
form each pair of opposite edges.
An AMC Upper Primary question can ask for
intersections, paths, or shapes cut out by grid lines.
Mark the object being counted.
A Rossmoyne style grid problem can require a shape to
include one marked cell while avoiding another.
Count by the possible boundaries.
The grid has three columns and two rows of squares.
How many points where vertical and horizontal lines
meet are there?
Count the lines along the outside edges too.
three columns need four vertical lines.
two rows need three horizontal lines.
Each vertical line crosses all three horizontal lines.
Multiply to get twelve crossing points.
A sheet has four columns and three rows of cells.
Count all rectangles whose sides lie along its grid
lines.
Rectangles can have any size.
A square counts too.
Choose two of the five vertical lines.
An unordered pair makes the left and right edge.
There are ten choices.
There are six horizontal pairs.
Choose one vertical pair and one horizontal pair
independently.
The four selected lines specify a unique rectangle.
Multiply the counts to get sixty.
On a six column by five row grid, cell A is in column
two, row three.
Rows are numbered from the bottom.
Cell B is in column five, row three.
Count the grid-line rectangles containing all of A but
none of the interior of B.
One way to begin is to count every rectangle containing
A.
Then identify the unwanted ones.
To contain A, the left and right edges have two and
five choices respectively.
The lower and upper edges have three and three choices.
That is ninety rectangles.
Each rectangle is counted once by the locations of its
four sides.
Now require it to contain both cells.
Each side must sit outside the smallest block that
contains A and B.
The edge counts for a rectangle enclosing both are two,
two, three and three.
Their product is thirty-six.
Subtract those from the count containing A.
Exactly fifty-four rectangles contain A and avoid B.
The outside boundary contributes two edge lines in each
direction.
A row of five cells sits between six lines.
For a rectangle, the pair of left and right lines has
no order to choose twice.
Choosing the lines fixes their order automatically.
Mark whether you are choosing lines, crossing points or
cells.
Count the outer boundaries before using a formula.
Set constraints on one edge choice at a time.
For a cell to be excluded, subtract exactly the choices
that include it.
